title: Hummingbirds: Ornery Helicopters of the Animal Kingdom
summary: Josh and Chuck explore hummingbirds: their weight and size, the 338 species found only in the Americas, their helicopter-like hovering flight, iridescent gorget feathers, extreme metabolism and daily food intake, torpor, migration (including the Gulf of Mexico crossing and the ruby-throated hummingbird east of the Mississippi), territoriality, the courtship dive and quick mating, nest-building with spider silk, feeding on nectar and insects, pollination in the Andes, and how to attract hummingbirds with flowers, feeders (sugar water ratio, avoiding red dye), and bird-friendly shade-grown coffee. The episode closes with a listener mail story about a birthmark that ruptured.

segments.title: Opening banter and hummingbird introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Josh's shaved beard and an owl attack in their neighborhood, then introduce hummingbirds, their family, size and weight, and the fact that their hovering flight is unusual.

segments.title: Hummingbird iridescence and species range
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the iridescent gorget feathers, which get their color from air bubbles in the feather structure rather than pigment, comparing it to butterfly wing iridescence. They cover the 338 species found in the Americas, their range from Chile to Alaska, and their adaptation to varied habitats.

segments.title: Hummingbird size and wing physiology
segments.summary: The hosts talk about the tiny bee hummingbird, the fact that no hummingbird species weighs an ounce, the ruby-throated hummingbird eggs, nests built with spider silk, and wing muscles making up a large share of body weight with weak legs.

segments.title: Hummingbird flight speed and heart rate
segments.summary: The hosts describe hummingbird flight abilities, including hovering, flying upside down and backward, speeds above 45 mph, heart rates, and wingbeats per second, plus the daily food intake of two to three times body weight.

segments.title: Hummingbird migration and torpor
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how hummingbirds time migration by flowering and possibly daylight, the bulk-up before migration, the ruby-throated hummingbird's Gulf of Mexico crossing, the 2016 study on flight range, and torpor as a deep sleep-like state. They also note Andean hummingbirds and the lack of insects above a certain elevation, making hummingbirds the sole pollinators there.

segments.title: Hummingbird territoriality, courtship, and mating
segments.summary: The hosts describe hummingbirds as unsociable and territorial because they must guard food sources. They explain the male courtship dive, the four-second mating on a branch, the female raising young alone, and how the male's bright gorget signals fitness.

segments.title: Hummingbird feeding, flowers, and feeders
segments.summary: The hosts explain the hummingbird's tube-like tongue for nectar, the insects it eats, the flowers it pollinates, and how to attract hummingbirds with hummingbird-friendly flowers such as cardinal flower, columbine, and coral honeysuckle. They also cover feeder sugar-water ratio and advice against red dye.

segments.title: Bird-friendly coffee
segments.summary: The hosts recommend bird-friendly, shade-grown, and rainforest alliance coffee as a way to help hummingbird habitat in the Andes-area coffee plantations.

segments.title: Legal note on harming hummingbirds
segments.summary: The hosts note that hummingbirds are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act and fines can reach two thousand dollars.

segments.title: Listener mail: exploding birthmark
segments.summary: Bailey writes about a childhood birthmark that ruptured as a vascular malformation on Thanksgiving, leading to surgery and a scar. The hosts react to the story.
